- **Refinement Ratio:** Assumed to be 2:1.
- **Standard Trilinear Failure:** Standard trilinear interpolation fails at level boundaries because not all 8 neighbors of a dual cell vertex exist or are at the same resolution.
- **Boundary Conditions:** The method assumes the query point is within the domain of the AMR hierarchy.
- **Time Complexity:** $O(1)$ per sample point after octant location.
The octant location is $O(\log N)$ where $N$ is the number of cells, but typically fast due to tree traversal.
The GTI step involves a fixed number of neighbor lookups and a dot product with 4 or 8 weights.
- **Memory Complexity:** $O(1)$ additional memory for precomputed weights (5 vectors of size 4, 20 vectors of size 8).
The main memory cost is the AMR data structure itself.
- **Limitations:** Requires precomputation of weights for all 20 3D cases; assumes 2:1 refinement ratio; more complex to implement than standard trilinear interpolation.
- **When to use:** When visualizing TB-AMR data with level boundaries and continuity is critical.
- **When not to use:** When the refinement ratio is not 2:1 (weights would need recomputation); when $C^0$ continuity is not required and simpler methods suffice.
GTI was introduced in 2020 by Wan et al. in the paper "CPU Ray Tracing of Tree-Based Adaptive Mesh Refinement Data" published in the Computer Graphics Forum.

It builds on prior work such as [ME11, WCM12, WBUK17, WWW*19] which proposed various approaches for stitching AMR data, but GTI specifically ensures $C^0$ continuity and adapts to the AMR mesh resolution to avoid artifacts.
